claims.text: Surface-driven atomic segregation governs premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation creates localized regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Localized surface regions with reduced cohesive energy act as nucleation sites for the liquid phase.
Heating drives surface segregation through surface-energy minimization.
Element-enriched surface regions have reduced local coordination and bonding energies.
Surface segregation causes melting to nucleate at lower temperatures than predicted by bulk phase data.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will exhibit an earlier onset of premelting than well-mixed nanoparticles.
Earlier premelting should appear as a lower-temperature DSC endotherm or as liquid-like surface layers in real-space TEM imaging.
Nanoparticles with homogeneous elemental distributions and minimal surface segregation should follow conventional premelting behavior predicted by bulk thermodynamics.
The proposed governing relationship should hold for nanoparticles below approximately 50 nm when oxidation and other extrinsic factors do not interfere.
Larger particles or particles with oxidized surfaces may deviate from the proposed relationship.
Tailored post-synthesis annealing can enhance surface segregation, whereas rapid quenching can maintain a more homogeneous surface.

A lack of a statistically significant difference in premelting onset or melting location between segregation-enhanced and homogeneous particles would falsify the proposed governing role of surface segregation.
